# How to use this guide

Introduction to Pharmacognosy is the first natural-products course of the new B.Pharm (NEP 2020) scheme. It is mostly a "learn and write" subject: definitions, classifications, tables of tests and short drug monographs. Study one unit at a time: read the notes, write the "Remember" list from memory, then answer the question bank. Each unit has very short (2-mark), short (4-mark) and long (8-mark) questions, rated by how likely that kind of question is.

The five units follow the five units of the PCI syllabus exactly; no unit was split or joined. Unit 4 is the largest (12 lectures) because it holds two topics — plant metabolites and traditional systems of medicine — so the notes treat them as two halves of one unit.

**End-semester paper (PCI B.Pharm 2026, NEP 2020, Table XV): 3-credit course, 45 marks, 2 hours.** Internal (sessional) assessment carries another 30 marks, making 75 for the course. Confirm the exact pattern with your university.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Multiple-choice questions — all compulsory | 10 × 1 = 10 |
| B | Short answers — attempt 5 of 7 | 5 × 4 = 20 |
| C | Long answers — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 7.5 = 15 |

**Note on the mock paper in this app**: the app can only give whole marks, so long answers are marked out of **8** in the mock paper and the total shows 46. Write each long answer as you would for 7.5 marks in the real paper.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — a question of this kind is very likely; prepare the full answer with a table or diagram.
- **Medium** — appears every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — less common, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from syllabus weight and the kinds of questions common in pharmacognosy papers. They are not a promise of what will be asked, especially since this is a new syllabus with few past papers.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics most likely to be asked |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Fundamentals | Definition, history and scope; classification of crude drugs with merits and limitations; sources of drugs; milestones (taxol, artemisinin, penicillin, morphine); herbal pharmacopoeias |
| 2 Cultivation | Methods of propagation; factors affecting cultivation; collection, drying and storage; WHO GACP; plant hormones; polyploidy/mutation/hybridisation; in-situ vs ex-situ conservation; kutki and chirata |
| 3 Quality control | Adulteration types with examples; methods of evaluation; ash and extractive values; stomatal index and other leaf constants; foaming index, swelling index, bitterness value; DNA barcoding |
| 4 Metabolites and traditional systems | Primary vs secondary metabolites; definition, properties and tests of alkaloids, glycosides, tannins, flavonoids, volatile oils, resins; principles of Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Homoeopathy, TCM; Ayurvedic dosage forms |
| 5 Phyto-therapeutic agents | Biological source, constituents and uses of any two or three drugs from the list (ashwagandha, turmeric, garlic, psyllium, vasaka and aloe are favourites) |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. **Biological source** must have three parts: the part used, the botanical name (underline it in a handwritten paper) and the family. "Turmeric is from *Curcuma longa*" alone loses marks; write "dried rhizomes of *Curcuma longa* L., family Zingiberaceae".
2. For **classification** questions, use a table with one example per class and one merit and one limitation for each system.
3. For **evaluation** questions, draw the five-branch chart (organoleptic, microscopic, physical, chemical, biological) first, then explain each with an example.
4. Learn the formulas exactly: stomatal index = S × 100/(E + S); foaming index = 1000/a; haemolytic activity = 1000a/b; bitterness value = 2000C/(A × B). A one-line worked example earns extra credit.
5. For **tests**, write reagent → observation → what it shows (Dragendorff's → orange-red precipitate → alkaloid).
6. For **traditional systems**, use a comparison table: basic theory, diagnosis, treatment and one dosage form for each system.
7. In 4-mark answers, aim for four clear points or a small table; in 7.5-mark answers, aim for a definition, a diagram or table, six to eight explained points and a short conclusion.
8. MCQs often test families and constituents: make your own flash cards from the summary table in Unit 5.

# Last-night revision sheet

## Unit 1 — Fundamentals

- Pharmacognosy = pharmakon (drug) + gnosis (knowledge); term credited to Seydler (1815). Dioscorides wrote *De Materia Medica*.
- Sources: plants, animals (honey, lanolin, gelatin), microbes (penicillin, streptomycin), marine (agar, trabectedin, ziconotide), minerals (kaolin, talc), plant tissue culture (shikonin).
- Milestones: morphine (Sertürner, first alkaloid) · quinine (Pelletier & Caventou, 1820) · aspirin (salicin of willow → Hoffmann, 1897) · warfarin (dicoumarol of spoiled sweet clover, Link) · penicillin (Fleming, 1928; Florey & Chain) · cephalosporin (Brotzu, Sardinia) · taxol (*Taxus brevifolia*, microtubule stabiliser) · artemisinin (Tu Youyou, *Artemisia annua*, Nobel 2015).
- Pharmacopoeias: IP (Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission), BHP, USP herbal and dietary supplement monographs, API and UPI (PCIM&H, Ministry of AYUSH), AHP (independent, USA).
- Official = in pharmacopoeia; codified = written in classical traditional texts; non-codified = folk/oral.
- Classifications: alphabetical · morphological (organised/unorganised) · taxonomical · chemical · pharmacological · chemotaxonomic.

## Unit 2 — Cultivation and conservation

- Propagation: seeds (cheap, variable) vs vegetative (cuttings, layering, grafting, budding, rhizomes, bulbs, micropropagation — true to type).
- Factors: altitude, temperature, rainfall, light, soil, fertiliser, pests, genetics.
- Collection: leaves at flowering · barks in spring · roots after aerial parts die · flowers as buds · gums in dry season.
- Drying stops enzymes and microbes; shade-dry aromatic drugs. Store cool, dry, dark, airtight.
- WHO GACP (2003): identity, seed, site, cultivation, harvest, processing, packing, personnel, documentation.
- Hormones: auxins (rooting), gibberellins (elongation, germination), cytokinins (shoots), ABA (dormancy), ethylene (ripening); jasmonate = elicitor.
- Colchicine → polyploidy; *Acorus calamus* ploidy changes β-asarone; mutation raised penicillin yield; peppermint is a natural hybrid.
- In-situ (reserves, sacred groves, MPCAs) vs ex-situ (gardens, seed banks, cryopreservation at −196 °C).
- Eco-pharmacognosy: sustainable sourcing. Kutki (*Picrorhiza kurroa*, picrosides) and chirata (*Swertia chirayita*, amarogentin, swertiamarin).

## Unit 3 — Quality control

- Adulteration: inferior varieties, look-alikes, exhausted drugs, artificial articles, heavy matter, synthetic principles, other parts (clove stalks, saffron stamens, safflower).
- Evaluation: organoleptic · microscopic · physical · chemical · biological.
- Stomatal index = S × 100/(E + S); vein-islet number, vein-termination number, palisade ratio; lycopodium ≈ 94,000 spores/mg.
- Stains: phloroglucinol + HCl (lignin, pink), iodine (starch, blue), Sudan III (oil, red), ruthenium red (mucilage).
- Ash: total (≤ 450 °C), acid-insoluble (sand), water-soluble. Extractive values: alcohol, water, ether.
- Foreign organic matter ≤ 2% (WHO general). Moisture: LOD at 105 °C; toluene distillation for oil drugs.
- Foaming index = 1000/a · haemolytic activity = 1000a/b · bitterness value vs quinine HCl (200,000) · swelling index = ml per 1 g.
- Acid value / saponification value = mg KOH per g oil. Optical rotation (polarimeter), refractive index (Abbe).
- DNA barcoding: rbcL, matK, ITS2, trnH–psbA — identity only, not potency.

## Unit 4 — Metabolites and traditional systems

- Primary (carbohydrates, proteins, lipids) vs secondary (alkaloids, glycosides, flavonoids, tannins, terpenoids, volatile oils, resins).
- Tests: Mayer's/Dragendorff's (alkaloids) · Borntrager's (anthraquinones) · Keller–Killiani (cardiac) · Shinoda (flavonoids) · FeCl3 + gelatin (tannins) · Molisch (sugars) · Biuret (protein) · Salkowski (sterols).
- Tannins: hydrolysable (gallic/ellagic; blue-black) vs condensed (catechin; green-black, phlobaphenes).
- Terpenoids: C10, C15 (artemisinin), C20 (taxol), C30 (boswellic acids), C40 (carotenoids).
- Resins: oleoresin, gum-resin, oleo-gum-resin, balsam (benzoic/cinnamic acid), glycoresin.
- Ayurveda: panchamahabhuta, tridosha (vata, pitta, kapha), panchakarma, rasayana. Unani: four humours, mizaj. Siddha: vatham, pitham, kabam. Homoeopathy: like cures like, potentisation. TCM: yin–yang, qi, five phases, acupuncture.
- Ayurvedic forms: swarasa, kalka, kwatha, hima, phanta, churna, vati, avaleha, asava/arishta (self-fermented), ghrita, taila, bhasma.

## Unit 5 — Phyto-therapeutic agents (drug · family · part · key constituent)

- Ashwagandha · Solanaceae · root · withaferin A | Tulsi · Lamiaceae · leaf · eugenol | Amla · Phyllanthaceae · fruit · vitamin C, emblicanins
- Milk thistle · Asteraceae · fruit · silymarin | Kutki · Plantaginaceae · rhizome · picrosides
- Garlic · Amaryllidaceae · bulb · alliin → allicin | Arjuna · Combretaceae · bark · arjunolic acid
- Gymnema · Apocynaceae · leaf · gymnemic acids | Fenugreek · Fabaceae · seed · 4-hydroxyisoleucine
- Turmeric · Zingiberaceae · rhizome · curcumin | Boswellia · Burseraceae · oleo-gum-resin · AKBA
- Brahmi · Plantaginaceae · herb · bacosides | Giloy · Menispermaceae · stem · tinosporide
- Neem · Meliaceae · leaf/seed · azadirachtin | Andrographis · Acanthaceae · aerial parts · andrographolide
- Psyllium · Plantaginaceae · seed/husk · arabinoxylan | Aloe · Asphodelaceae · gel/latex · acemannan, aloin
- Chasteberry · Lamiaceae · fruit · agnuside | Shatavari · Asparagaceae · root · shatavarins | Vasaka · Acanthaceae · leaf · vasicine (→ bromhexine)

questions.answer:
1. Definition: pharmacognosy (pharmakon = drug, gnosis = knowledge) is the study of drugs of natural origin — their sources, identification, cultivation, constituents, evaluation and uses.
2. Alphabetical: drugs listed A to Z by Latin/English name (acacia, agar, aloe…), as in IP and BP. Merit: quick to locate. Limitation: no relationship between drugs.
3. Morphological: by part used — organised drugs (leaves: senna; barks: cinchona; roots: rauwolfia; flowers: clove; fruits: fennel; seeds: nux vomica) and unorganised drugs (gums, resins, latex, oils, extracts). Merit: helps identification and practical study. Limitation: ignores chemistry and action.
4. Taxonomical: by natural plant classification — family, genus, species (Solanaceae: belladonna, datura; Apiaceae: fennel, coriander). Merit: shows natural relationship; related plants often share constituents. Limitation: no link to therapeutic use; changes with revision of families.
5. Chemical: by main constituent — alkaloids (cinchona), glycosides (senna), tannins (catechu), volatile oils (clove), resins (benzoin), carbohydrates (acacia). Merit: suits phytochemical study and assays. Limitation: drugs with several constituent groups; some constituents unknown.
6. Pharmacological: by action — laxatives (senna, ispaghula), cardiotonics (digitalis, arjuna), expectorants (vasaka), hepatoprotectives (milk thistle). Merit: useful for clinical use and substitutes. Limitation: one drug with several actions; unrelated plants together.
7. Chemotaxonomic: by botanical relationship plus chemistry (tropane alkaloids in Solanaceae, isoquinolines in Papaveraceae). Merit: modern, finds new sources and corrects taxonomy. Limitation: needs complete chemical data; compounds can occur in unrelated families.
8. Conclusion: no single system is perfect; morphological suits identification, chemical and pharmacological suit study of action.
questions.question: Define pharmacognosy. Describe the different systems of classification of crude drugs with suitable examples, giving the merits and limitations of each.

questions.answer:
1. History: ancient Indian texts (Charaka, Sushruta Samhita), Chinese herbal tradition, Egyptian Ebers Papyrus; Dioscorides' De Materia Medica (1st century AD); Galen (galenicals); Avicenna's Canon; term pharmacognosy credited to Seydler (1815); 19th-century isolation of pure principles.
2. Present status: many modern drugs are natural or nature-derived (anticancer, antibiotics); large population uses traditional medicine; AYUSH herbal industry; herbal products need regulation and quality control.
3. Scope: authentication, standardisation and QC; cultivation and conservation (GACP); phytochemistry; drug discovery; biotechnology and tissue culture; herbal formulations; pharmacovigilance; nutraceuticals and cosmetics; pharmacopoeial and regulatory work.
4. Morphine: from opium poppy latex, isolated by Sertürner in the early 1800s — first alkaloid; still a standard analgesic.
5. Quinine: from cinchona bark, isolated by Pelletier and Caventou (1820) — first effective antimalarial, led to chloroquine.
6. Penicillin: Fleming (1928) observed Penicillium notatum killing staphylococci; Florey and Chain purified it — start of the antibiotic era.
7. Artemisinin: Tu Youyou isolated it from Artemisia annua (qinghao) guided by an old Chinese text; sesquiterpene lactone endoperoxide; artemisinin combinations treat falciparum malaria (Nobel 2015).
8. (Alternatives: aspirin from salicin of willow, warfarin from dicoumarol of spoiled sweet clover, cephalosporin from Brotzu's fungus, taxol from Taxus brevifolia.)
questions.question: Write a note on the history, present status and scope of pharmacognosy. Add an account of any four historical milestones in drug discovery from natural sources.

questions.answer:
1. Plants — largest source: morphine (opium poppy), digoxin (Digitalis lanata), quinine (cinchona).
2. Animals: honey, beeswax, lanolin, gelatin, cod-liver oil.
3. Microbes (fermentation): penicillin (Penicillium), streptomycin (Streptomyces griseus), lovastatin (Aspergillus terreus).
4. Marine: agar and alginates (seaweeds), trabectedin (sea squirt), ziconotide (cone snail).
5. Minerals: kaolin, talc, calcium carbonate, bhasmas.
6. Plant tissue culture: shikonin from Lithospermum cell culture; paclitaxel by plant cell fermentation.
questions.question: Describe the various sources of drugs of natural origin with two examples of each.

questions.answer:
1. Source: bark of the Pacific yew, Taxus brevifolia (Taxaceae).
2. Found in a US National Cancer Institute plant-screening programme; isolated by Wall and Wani; a diterpenoid.
3. Unique action: binds tubulin and stabilises microtubules, stopping cell division (mitotic arrest).
4. Supply problem: bark of slow-growing trees gave tiny yields and killed the tree.
5. Solution: semisynthesis from 10-deacetylbaccatin III obtained from renewable needles of Taxus baccata; also plant cell fermentation.
6. Use: ovarian, breast and lung cancers. Lesson: natural lead + conservation through semisynthesis.
questions.question: Write a short note on the discovery of taxol (paclitaxel).

questions.answer:
1. Pharmacopoeia = official book of standards giving monographs for identity, purity and strength.
2. Indian Pharmacopoeia — Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (first edition 1955); legal standard under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act; has herbal monographs (macroscopy, microscopy, TLC, ash, extractives, marker assay).
3. British Herbal Pharmacopoeia — British Herbal Medicine Association; monographs for herbal practitioners.
4. USP Herbal Medicines and Dietary Supplements — monographs for botanicals and their extracts.
5. Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India and Unani Pharmacopoeia of India — PCIM&H, Ministry of AYUSH; single drugs and formulations with traditional properties.
6. American Herbal Pharmacopoeia — independent US body; detailed botanical, analytical and therapeutic monographs, not legally binding.
questions.question: Write a note on herbal and traditional pharmacopoeias.

questions.answer:
1. Official drug: has a monograph in the official pharmacopoeia and must meet its standards (ispaghula husk, senna in IP).
2. Non-official drug: not in the pharmacopoeia, though it may be widely used (many folk herbs).
3. Codified drug: use recorded in authoritative classical texts of a traditional system — Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha (Triphala churna, Ashwagandharishta).
4. Non-codified drug: folk, tribal or household remedies passed on orally, not in classical texts; need documentation (Traditional Knowledge Digital Library) and are leads for ethnopharmacology.
questions.question: Differentiate between official and non-official drugs, and between codified and non-codified drugs, with examples.

questions.answer: Crude drug: a natural product only collected and dried or simply processed, not purified (senna leaf). Biological source: the plant or animal giving the drug, stated with part used, botanical name and family (clove = dried flower buds of Syzygium aromaticum, Myrtaceae).
questions.question: Define crude drug and biological source.

questions.answer: Organised drugs have a cellular structure and are plant or animal parts (senna leaf, cinchona bark). Unorganised drugs have no cells: gums, resins, latex, dried juices, oils and extracts (acacia gum, aloe).
questions.question: What are organised and unorganised drugs? Give one example of each.

questions.answer:
1. Sexual (seed) propagation: fennel, coriander, isabgol, datura; cheap and easy, hardy plants, but offspring vary; seed treatments — soaking, scarification, stratification, gibberellic acid.
2. Vegetative — natural: rhizomes (ginger, turmeric), bulbs (garlic), tubers, runners and suckers (mint).
3. Vegetative — artificial: cuttings (stem, root — rauwolfia), layering (simple, air layering/gootee), grafting (scion on rootstock), budding.
4. Micropropagation: explants on sterile medium with auxin and cytokinin give many identical plantlets (rare plants, kutki).
5. Merits of vegetative methods: true-to-type plants with uniform chemistry, early maturity; demerits: costly, disease carried over.
6. Factors: altitude (tea, cinchona, Himalayan kutki), temperature, rainfall and irrigation, day length and light, soil (texture, pH, drainage).
7. Fertilisers and manures (nitrogen raises alkaloid content in belladonna), pests and diseases, genetic make-up (chemotypes).
8. Conclusion: cultivation of authenticated material under GACP gives uniform quality and protects wild stocks.
questions.question: Describe the methods of propagation of medicinal plants. Discuss the factors influencing the cultivation of medicinal plants.

questions.answer:
1. Conservation: protection and sustainable use of medicinal plant resources so that they remain for future use; needed because most raw material is collected from the wild and many species are threatened (IUCN Red List, CITES, NMPB, Biological Diversity Act 2002).
2. In-situ: in natural habitat — national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, sacred groves, Medicinal Plants Conservation Areas; keeps whole ecosystem; needs protection from people.
3. Ex-situ: outside habitat — botanical/herbal gardens, field gene banks, seed banks, tissue culture, cryopreservation (−196 °C), farm cultivation; rescues rare species, but limited genetic diversity and costly.
4. Value addition: processing, standardised extracts, certification, producer groups — gives farmers reason to cultivate.
5. Eco-pharmacognosy: sustainable use of natural resources for medicines — cultivation instead of wild collection, limits on harvesting, use of renewable parts, biotechnology, benefit sharing.
6. Kutki (Picrorhiza kurroa, Plantaginaceae): alpine Himalayan; rhizome with picrosides (kutkin); threatened by uprooting; conserved by cultivation, micropropagation, nurseries and harvest limits.
7. Chirata (Swertia chirayita, Gentianaceae): whole plant; amarogentin, swertiamarin, mangiferin; uprooted before seed set and widely substituted; conserved by seed cultivation, tissue culture and harvesting after seed fall.
questions.question: What is conservation of medicinal plants? Compare in-situ and ex-situ conservation. Explain the role of eco-pharmacognosy in conserving kutki and chirata.

questions.answer:
1. Correct botanical identification; voucher specimens; authentic, disease-free seed and planting material.
2. Site free from heavy metals, pesticides and pollution; suitable climate.
3. Composted manure only, clean irrigation water, minimum approved pesticides with records.
4. Harvest at the right stage in dry weather with clean equipment; wild collection with permits and sustainable quantities.
5. Prompt primary processing (cleaning, drying); clean packaging, labelled storage and transport.
6. Trained, healthy personnel with hygiene; full documentation and traceability; quality assurance and audits.
questions.question: Write the WHO guidelines on Good Agricultural and Collection Practices (GACP) for medicinal plants.

questions.answer:
1. Collection time: leaves at flowering; flowers before full opening (clove buds); barks in spring when cambium is active; roots and rhizomes after aerial parts die; seeds when ripe; gums in the dry season.
2. Processing: garbling to remove foreign matter, washing, slicing, special treatments (peeling, curing of vanilla, boiling of turmeric).
3. Drying stops enzyme and microbial action: sun drying (seeds, roots), shade drying (aromatic and coloured drugs), artificial driers at controlled temperature, freeze-drying.
4. Storage: cool, dry, dark, ventilated store; airtight containers; desiccant for hygroscopic drugs (squill, digitalis); amber containers for light-sensitive drugs; protection from insects (fumigation) and rodents; first-in-first-out and labelling.

1. Auxins (IAA, IBA, NAA): rooting of stem cuttings; callus formation in tissue culture; 2,4-D as weedicide.
2. Gibberellins (GA3): break seed dormancy, improve germination, stem elongation and biomass.
3. Cytokinins (kinetin, BAP, zeatin): cell division and shoot multiplication in micropropagation (high cytokinin → shoots, high auxin → roots).
4. Abscisic acid: dormancy and stress response; ethylene/ethephon: ripening, increased latex flow (rubber).
5. Elicitors such as methyl jasmonate and salicylic acid raise secondary metabolite yield in cell cultures.
questions.question: Write the applications of plant hormones in the cultivation of medicinal plants.

questions.answer:
1. Polyploidy: more than two chromosome sets, induced by colchicine (blocks spindle formation); larger organs, often more constituent; tetraploid Datura with more alkaloid; Acorus calamus ploidy decides β-asarone content.
2. Mutation: heritable change induced by X-rays, gamma rays, UV or chemicals (EMS); high-yield mutants selected — Penicillium chrysogenum strains raised penicillin yield many-fold; thebaine-rich poppy lines.
3. Hybridisation: crossing varieties or species to combine characters; Cinchona ledgeriana × C. succirubra; peppermint is a natural hybrid of water mint and spearmint; hybrid vigour.
4. All three need screening and stabilisation of the improved plants.
questions.question: Explain the application of polyploidy, mutation and hybridisation in improving the yield of secondary metabolites.

questions.answer: Eco-pharmacognosy is the study and practice of sourcing medicines from nature in a sustainable, environment-friendly way — cultivation, controlled harvesting, renewable parts, biotechnology and benefit sharing — so medicinal species survive for future generations.
questions.question: What is eco-pharmacognosy?

questions.answer: Chirata is the dried whole plant of Swertia chirayita, family Gentianaceae; constituents include the bitter secoiridoid glycosides amarogentin and swertiamarin, and the xanthone mangiferin.
questions.question: Give the biological source and one constituent of chirata.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: substitution of the genuine drug, fully or partly, with other material, or addition of material that lowers its quality, purity or strength; may be intentional or unintentional.
2. Reasons: scarcity and high price, confusion of vernacular names, similar appearance, careless collection, profit.
3. Inferior commercial varieties: Arabian senna for Indian senna; Strychnos nux-blanda for nux vomica.
4. Superficially similar inferior drugs: Ailanthus or Phytolacca leaves in belladonna; papaya seeds in black pepper.
5. Exhausted drugs: clove and ginger after oil extraction; saffron re-dyed after extraction.
6. Artificially made substitutes: moulded artificial coffee beans or nutmeg.
7. Worthless heavy materials: sand in saffron, stones in liquorice, brick powder in powders; synthetic principles: citral in lemon oil, benzyl benzoate in balsam of Peru.
8. Other parts of the same plant: clove stalks and mother cloves; saffron stamens; stems with senna leaves; foreign florets (safflower in saffron). Detection: organoleptic, microscopic, physical, chemical and DNA methods.
questions.question: Define adulteration. Describe the different types of adulteration of crude drugs with suitable examples.

questions.answer:
1. Evaluation = confirming identity and judging quality and purity of a drug; five methods.
2. Organoleptic: colour, odour, taste, size, shape, fracture, special features (quills of cinnamon, bitter taste of chirata).
3. Microscopic: qualitative (trichomes, stomata, calcium oxalate crystals, starch, fibres; stains such as phloroglucinol-HCl, iodine, Sudan III) and quantitative (stomatal index, vein-islet number, palisade ratio, lycopodium spore method).
4. Physical: moisture, ash, extractive values, viscosity, swelling index, optical rotation, refractive index, melting point.
5. Chemical: identity tests (Dragendorff's, Borntrager's, Keller–Killiani), constants (acid and saponification values), assays (titration, UV, HPLC), fingerprints (TLC, HPTLC).
6. Biological: bioassay against a standard (digitalis in pigeon or guinea pig), microbial assay of antibiotics, microbial limit tests; also heavy metals, pesticides, aflatoxins.
7. Ash values: total ash (incineration ≤ 450 °C, all inorganic matter), acid-insoluble ash (residue insoluble in dilute HCl — sand and silica), water-soluble ash (detects water-exhausted drug), sulphated ash.
8. Extractive values: alcohol-soluble (5 g macerated in 100 ml ethanol 24 h, 20 ml filtrate evaporated, dried at 105 °C), water-soluble, ether-soluble; low values indicate exhausted or adulterated drug and are used when no assay exists.
questions.question: Describe the methods of evaluation of crude drugs. Explain ash values and extractive values.

questions.answer:
1. Stomatal index = percentage proportion of stomata to the total number of epidermal cells (each stoma counted as one cell) in a given area.
2. SI = S × 100 / (E + S), where S = number of stomata and E = number of epidermal cells.
3. Method: peel or clear a leaf piece with chloral hydrate, mount, use a camera lucida/eyepiece grid, count stomata and epidermal cells in several fields and average.
4. Calculation: SI = 18 × 100 / (82 + 18) = 1800/100 = 18.
5. Significance: fairly constant for a species, used to distinguish related leaves (Indian and Alexandrian senna).
questions.question: Define stomatal index. How is it determined? Calculate the stomatal index if 18 stomata and 82 epidermal cells are counted in a field.

questions.answer:
1. Foaming index: measures saponin content by persistent foam; a decoction is put in tubes in increasing volumes made up to 10 ml, each shaken 15 s, left 15 min, foam height read.
2. Foaming index = 1000/a, where a = ml of decoction in the tube with 1 cm foam (below 1 cm in all tubes → reported as less than 100). Used for liquorice, shatavari, quillaia.
3. Swelling index: volume in ml occupied by 1 g of drug with its adhering mucilage after swelling in water for a stated time in a measuring cylinder.
4. Used for mucilage drugs — ispaghula, linseed, fenugreek; a low value shows adulteration or old material.
questions.question: Explain foaming index and swelling index with their significance.

questions.answer:
1. DNA barcoding identifies a species from a short standard DNA region.
2. Steps: DNA extraction → PCR amplification of barcode → sequencing → comparison with a reference library.
3. Plant barcodes: rbcL and matK (core), ITS/ITS2, trnH–psbA.
4. Uses: identify powdered/cut drugs, detect substitution in herbal products, check trade in endangered species; independent of season and plant part.
5. Limitations: gives identity not potency; DNA degraded in processed extracts; needs reference data and laboratory.
questions.question: Write a note on DNA barcoding of herbal drugs.

questions.answer:
1. Acid value: mg of KOH needed to neutralise the free fatty acids in 1 g of fat or oil.
2. Significance: high acid value means hydrolysis and rancidity on storage.
3. Saponification value: mg of KOH needed to saponify the esters (and neutralise free acids) in 1 g of fat or oil.
4. Significance: inversely related to mean molecular weight of fatty acids; falls when unsaponifiable mineral oil is added — detects adulteration.
5. Ester value = saponification value − acid value.
questions.question: Define acid value and saponification value. What is their significance in evaluation of oils?

questions.answer: Acid-insoluble ash is the part of total ash that does not dissolve on boiling with dilute hydrochloric acid. It is mostly silica, so a high value shows contamination with sand, soil or earthy matter.
questions.question: What is acid-insoluble ash? What does a high value indicate?

questions.answer: Lycopodium spores are uniform, about 94,000 per mg. A known weight is mixed with a known weight of powdered drug; counting characteristic drug particles and spores in the same fields allows calculation of the percentage of genuine drug.
questions.question: State the principle of the lycopodium spore method.

questions.answer:
1. Primary metabolites: essential for life, found in all plants, large amounts, made by photosynthesis and central metabolism — carbohydrates, proteins, lipids; used as excipients and nutrients.
2. Secondary metabolites: not essential, limited distribution, small amounts, defence and attraction roles, made via shikimic acid, acetate–malonate and mevalonate/MEP pathways — alkaloids, glycosides, tannins, flavonoids, terpenoids; mostly the active drugs.
3. Alkaloids: basic nitrogenous compounds, nitrogen usually in a heterocyclic ring, of plant origin, with marked physiological action.
4. Properties: mostly crystalline, bitter, bases soluble in organic solvents and salts in water, form salts with acids, optically active; nicotine and coniine are liquids.
5. Tests: Mayer's (cream ppt), Dragendorff's (orange-red), Wagner's (reddish-brown), Hager's (yellow); examples morphine, quinine, atropine, reserpine, vasicine.
6. Glycosides: give a sugar (glycone) and a non-sugar aglycone on hydrolysis; O-, C-, S- and N-glycosides; water-soluble, bitter, hydrolysed by acids and enzymes.
7. Classes and tests: anthraquinone (senna — Borntrager's, pink ammonia layer), cardiac (digitalis — Keller–Killiani), saponin (froth test, haemolysis), cyanogenetic (picrate paper brick red), flavonoid (Shinoda).
questions.question: Differentiate between primary and secondary metabolites. Give the definition, general properties and tests of alkaloids and glycosides.

questions.answer:
1. Ayurveda: panchamahabhuta (five elements), tridosha — vata, pitta, kapha; saptadhatu, agni, prakriti; treatment by shodhana (panchakarma: vamana, virechana, basti, nasya, raktamokshana), shamana (drugs, diet), rasayana.
2. Unani: four humours (dam, balgham, safra, sauda); mizaj (temperament); tabiyat (healing power); ilaj-bil-tadbeer, ilaj-bil-ghiza, ilaj-bil-dawa, jarahat.
3. Siddha: Tamil system of the Siddhars; vatham, pitham, kabam; envagai thervu (eight-fold diagnosis); herbs plus purified metals and minerals.
4. Homoeopathy: Hahnemann; similia similibus curentur; drug proving, single remedy, minimum dose, potentisation, individualisation.
5. TCM: yin–yang balance, qi in meridians, five phases; herbal formulas, acupuncture, moxibustion, cupping, qigong.
6. Role of pharmacognosy: authentication of herbs with confusing names; standardisation and monographs (API, UPI); detection of adulteration (microscopy, HPTLC, DNA barcoding).
7. Safety testing (heavy metals, pesticides, microbes, aflatoxins); scientific validation and reverse pharmacology; cultivation and conservation; modern dosage forms.
questions.question: Explain the basic principles of treatment in Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Homoeopathy and Traditional Chinese Medicine. Add a note on the role of pharmacognosy in traditional systems of medicine.

questions.answer:
1. Tannins: polyphenols that precipitate proteins and tan hide; astringent.
2. Hydrolysable: esters of gallic or ellagic acid with sugar, hydrolysed by acids/enzymes; blue-black with FeCl3 (myrobalan, amla, nutgall).
3. Condensed (proanthocyanidins): polymers of flavan-3-ols, not hydrolysed, form red phlobaphenes with acid; green-black with FeCl3 (catechu, tea, arjuna).
4. Pseudotannins: small phenolics (gallic acid, chlorogenic acid).
5. Tests: gelatin precipitate, goldbeater's skin test, ferric chloride.
6. Uses: astringent in diarrhoea and bleeding gums, wound healing, antioxidant, leather tanning.
questions.question: Classify tannins. Give their tests and uses.

questions.answer:
1. Resins: amorphous, water-insoluble, alcohol-soluble plant products, mostly from oxidised terpenes; soften on heating, burn with smoky flame.
2. Hard resins: colophony.
3. Oleoresins (resin + volatile oil): turpentine, ginger oleoresin, capsicum.
4. Gum-resins (resin + gum): myrrh.
5. Oleo-gum-resins: asafoetida, boswellia, guggul.
6. Balsams (contain benzoic and/or cinnamic acid): benzoin, tolu, Peru balsam.
7. Glycoresins: jalap.
questions.question: Write the classification of resins with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Panchavidha kashaya kalpana: swarasa (expressed juice), kalka (paste), kwatha (decoction), hima (cold infusion), phanta (hot infusion).
2. Churna (powder — Triphala churna); vati/gutika (pills); avaleha (semisolid confection — Chyawanprash).
3. Asava and arishta: self-fermented liquids whose alcohol forms during fermentation; asava from juice/cold infusion, arishta from decoction.
4. Ghrita (medicated ghee), taila (medicated oil).
5. Bhasma (calcined metals/minerals), guggulu preparations, arka (distillate), lepa (external paste).
questions.question: Describe the types of dosage forms used in Ayurveda.

questions.answer:
1. Volatile oils: odorous oily liquids of plant origin that evaporate at room temperature; mixtures of terpenes and phenylpropanoids.
2. Properties: volatile, spot on paper disappears; mostly lighter than water (clove oil heavier); high refractive index; optically active; soluble in alcohol, slightly in water; resinify and darken in air and light.
3. Occur in glandular hairs, oil cells, ducts and glands; extracted by steam distillation, expression or enfleurage.
4. Examples: clove oil (eugenol), peppermint oil (menthol), eucalyptus (cineole).
5. Uses: carminative, flavour, perfume, antiseptic.
questions.question: Define volatile oils. Write their general properties and two examples.

questions.answer: Flavonoids are polyphenolic plant pigments with a C6–C3–C6 skeleton (quercetin, rutin, silybin). Shinoda test: magnesium turnings and concentrated HCl give a pink to red colour.
questions.question: What are flavonoids? Name the test for flavonoids.

questions.answer: AYUSH stands for Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy (Sowa-Rigpa is also recognised); the Ministry of AYUSH governs these systems in India.
questions.question: What is AYUSH?

questions.answer:
1. Ashwagandha: dried roots of Withania somnifera (L.) Dunal, family Solanaceae.
2. Constituents: withanolides (withaferin A, withanolide D), sitoindosides, alkaloids (withanine, somniferine), starch.
3. Uses: adaptogen, anti-stress, rasayana, immunomodulator, general and nervine tonic, weakness, insomnia; Ashwagandharishta.
4. Tulsi: leaves of Ocimum tenuiflorum L. (O. sanctum), family Lamiaceae.
5. Constituents: volatile oil with eugenol, methyl eugenol, caryophyllene; ursolic acid; rosmarinic acid; flavonoids. Uses: adaptogen, immunomodulator, cough, cold, fever, antimicrobial.
6. Amla: fruits of Emblica officinalis Gaertn. (Phyllanthus emblica), family Phyllanthaceae.
7. Constituents: vitamin C, hydrolysable tannins (emblicanin A and B), gallic and ellagic acids, pectin. Uses: antioxidant, rasayana, immunity, scurvy, hair tonic; in Triphala and Chyawanprash.
questions.question: Write the biological source, chemical constituents and uses of ashwagandha, tulsi and amla.

questions.answer:
1. Milk thistle: dried ripe fruits of Silybum marianum (L.) Gaertn., family Asteraceae.
2. Constituents: silymarin — flavonolignans silybin (silibinin), isosilybin, silychristin, silydianin; fixed oil. Uses: alcoholic and drug-induced liver damage, fatty liver, cirrhosis; antioxidant, membrane stabiliser; silibinin as adjunct in Amanita mushroom poisoning.
3. Kutki: rhizomes and roots of Picrorhiza kurroa Royle ex Benth., family Plantaginaceae.
4. Constituents: iridoid glycosides picroside I, picroside II, kutkoside (kutkin), apocynin, cucurbitacins. Uses: hepatoprotective in jaundice, choleretic, bitter stomachic, antipyretic, immunomodulator.
5. Garlic: bulbs of Allium sativum L., family Amaryllidaceae.
6. Constituents: alliin converted by alliinase on crushing to allicin, which forms ajoene and diallyl di-/trisulfides.
7. Uses: lowers cholesterol and triglycerides, antiplatelet, mild antihypertensive, antimicrobial, expectorant, carminative; may add to bleeding risk with anticoagulants.
questions.question: Give the biological source, constituents and uses of hepatoprotective drugs milk thistle and kutki, and of the cardiovascular drug garlic.

questions.answer:
1. Biological source: dried, boiled rhizomes of Curcuma longa L., family Zingiberaceae.
2. Constituents: curcuminoids — curcumin, demethoxycurcumin, bisdemethoxycurcumin; volatile oil (turmerone, ar-turmerone, zingiberene); starch.
3. Uses: anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antiseptic, wound healing, skin care, hepatoprotective, carminative; colour and spice.
4. Note: poor absorption of curcumin, improved with piperine; test — conc. H2SO4 gives crimson colour.
questions.question: Write the biological source, constituents and uses of turmeric.

questions.answer:
1. Biological source: dried ripe seeds and seed husk of Plantago ovata Forssk., family Plantaginaceae.
2. Constituents: mucilage (arabinoxylan) in the epidermis of the seed coat; fixed oil and proteins in the kernel.
3. Uses: bulk laxative in constipation; diarrhoea and IBS (forms gel); lowers cholesterol; piles and fissure.
4. Must be taken with plenty of water; quality checked by swelling index.
questions.question: Write the biological source, constituents and uses of psyllium (isabgol).

questions.answer:
1. Biological source: leaves of Justicia adhatoda L. (Adhatoda vasica Nees), family Acanthaceae.
2. Constituents: quinazoline alkaloids vasicine and vasicinone, vasicol, volatile oil, betaine.
3. Uses: expectorant and bronchodilator in cough, bronchitis and asthma; vasaka syrup, Vasavaleha.
4. Vasicine served as the model for bromhexine and its metabolite ambroxol.
questions.question: Write a note on vasaka.

questions.answer:
1. Source: leaves of Aloe vera (L.) Burm.f. (A. barbadensis), family Asphodelaceae; gel from inner leaf tissue and dried latex (aloe) from cut leaves.
2. Gel constituents: acemannan (acetylated glucomannan), glycoproteins, enzymes, vitamins.
3. Latex constituents: anthrone C-glycoside aloin (barbaloin), aloe-emodin, resins.
4. Uses: gel for burns, sunburn, wounds, moisturiser; latex as stimulant purgative; borax test gives green fluorescence.
questions.question: Write the biological source, constituents and uses of aloe.

questions.answer:
1. Boswellia: oleo-gum-resin from the bark of Boswellia serrata, family Burseraceae; boswellic acids including AKBA, gum, volatile oil.
2. Uses: anti-inflammatory in osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease; inhibits 5-lipoxygenase.
3. Brahmi: whole herb of Bacopa monnieri, family Plantaginaceae; bacosides A and B (dammarane saponins), brahmine.
4. Uses: memory enhancer (medhya rasayana), anxiolytic, nervine tonic; not to be confused with Centella asiatica (also called brahmi).
questions.question: Write the biological source, constituents and uses of boswellia and brahmi.

questions.answer: Gymnemic acids (triterpenoid saponins) and the polypeptide gurmarin; chewing the leaves suppresses the sweet taste, and the drug lowers blood sugar.

units.markdown:
# Unit 1: Fundamentals of pharmacognosy

Pharmacognosy is the oldest branch of pharmacy. Before chemists could make medicines in a flask, every medicine came from a plant, an animal or a mineral. This unit explains what the subject is, where crude drugs come from, how a few famous natural products changed medicine, which official books describe herbal drugs, and how crude drugs are classified. Expect one long answer from this unit (classification, or history and scope) and two or three short answers or MCQs on pharmacopoeias and drug discovery.

## 1.1 Definition

The word comes from two Greek words: **pharmakon** = drug and **gnosis** = knowledge. So pharmacognosy literally means "knowledge of drugs".

**Pharmacognosy** is the study of drugs of natural origin (plants, animals, micro-organisms, marine organisms and minerals): their sources, identification, cultivation, collection, preparation, chemical constituents, quality evaluation, uses and conservation.

Key terms:

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Crude drug | A natural product that has only been collected and dried (or given simple treatment such as cutting or powdering); not purified. Example: senna leaf, clove bud |
| Biological source | The plant or animal that gives the drug, written with its botanical (Latin) name and family. Example: clove = dried flower buds of *Syzygium aromaticum*, family Myrtaceae |
| Geographical source | The region where the drug is grown or collected |
| Active constituent | The chemical responsible for the drug's action. Example: hyoscyamine in belladonna |
| Phytochemistry | Chemistry of plant constituents: their extraction, isolation, structure and biosynthesis |
| Herbal drug / phytomedicine | A medicine whose active part is a plant material or its extract |

## 1.2 History of pharmacognosy

```text
Ancient texts ──► Greek & Roman materia medica ──► Arab scholars ──► 19th-century chemistry ──► Modern pharmacognosy
(Ayurveda, China,   (Hippocrates, Dioscorides,       (Avicenna,       (isolation of morphine,      (phytochemistry,
 Egypt)              Galen)                            Unani system)     quinine; the word           biotechnology,
                                                                         "pharmacognosy")            standardisation)
```

- **Ancient India**: the Vedas, and later the *Charaka Samhita* (medicine) and *Sushruta Samhita* (surgery), describe hundreds of medicinal plants and how to prepare them.
- **China**: the herbal attributed to the legendary emperor Shen Nong lists several hundred drugs; Traditional Chinese Medicine grew from these texts.
- **Egypt**: the *Ebers Papyrus* (about 1500 BC) records drugs such as castor oil, aloe and opium.
- **Greece and Rome**: **Hippocrates** (often called the father of medicine) used plant remedies; **Dioscorides** wrote *De Materia Medica* (1st century AD), describing about 600 plants — the main reference on drugs for more than 1,500 years; **Galen** gave his name to "galenical" preparations (extracts and tinctures made by simple methods).
- **Arab period**: **Avicenna (Ibn Sina)** wrote the *Canon of Medicine*; Arab physicians developed distillation, syrups and the Unani system.
- **Origin of the word**: the term "pharmacognosy" came into use in the early 19th century; it is usually credited to **C. A. Seydler** (1815, *Analectica Pharmacognostica*), with J. A. Schmidt having used a similar term a few years earlier.
- **19th century**: chemists isolated pure active principles — morphine, quinine, strychnine, atropine — and pharmacognosy moved from describing the outer look of drugs to studying their chemistry.

## 1.3 Present status and scope

Pharmacognosy today is no longer only "drug identification". It joins botany, chemistry, pharmacology and biotechnology.

**Present status**

- A large share of modern medicines are natural products, or are derived from or modelled on them, especially anticancer drugs and antibiotics.
- The World Health Organization accepts that a large part of the world's population depends on traditional medicine for primary health care.
- India has a strong herbal industry under the Ministry of AYUSH, and is among the leading exporters of medicinal plants and extracts.
- Herbal drugs are now sold as medicines, dietary supplements, nutraceuticals and cosmetics, so their quality control has become a regulatory need.

**Scope** (where a pharmacognosist works)

1. **Identification and authentication** of crude drugs, including detection of adulteration (microscopy, chromatographic fingerprints, DNA barcoding).
2. **Standardisation and quality control** of herbal raw materials and finished products.
3. **Cultivation and conservation** of medicinal plants; Good Agricultural and Collection Practices.
4. **Phytochemistry**: extraction, isolation and structure of active constituents.
5. **Drug discovery**: natural products as leads for new medicines (taxol, artemisinin).
6. **Biotechnology**: plant tissue culture, genetic improvement, microbial production of drugs.
7. **Herbal formulation**: tablets, capsules, creams and standardised extracts.
8. **Pharmacovigilance and herb–drug interactions** of herbal medicines.
9. **Nutraceuticals, cosmetics, food colours and flavours** of natural origin.
10. **Regulatory work**: writing monographs for pharmacopoeias, export and import quality certificates.

**Development of pharmacognosy** in short: descriptive (morphology) → analytical (microscopy, chemistry) → experimental (biosynthesis, tissue culture) → molecular (DNA methods, genomics, metabolomics).

## 1.4 Sources of drugs

| Source | Examples | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Plants** | Morphine (opium poppy), digoxin (*Digitalis lanata*), quinine (cinchona bark), reserpine (*Rauwolfia*), vincristine (*Catharanthus*), senna, ispaghula | Largest source; any part may be used — leaf, bark, root, rhizome, flower, fruit, seed, whole plant, exudate |
| **Animals** | Honey, beeswax, lanolin (wool fat), gelatin, cod-liver oil, shark-liver oil, musk, insulin (earlier from pancreas), heparin | Give fats, waxes, proteins, hormones |
| **Microbes** | Penicillin (*Penicillium*), streptomycin (*Streptomyces griseus*), cephalosporins, ergot alkaloids (*Claviceps purpurea*), lovastatin (*Aspergillus terreus*) | Grown by fermentation, so supply is steady |
| **Marine** | Agar and alginates (seaweeds), cytarabine (modelled on nucleosides from a marine sponge), trabectedin (sea squirt), ziconotide (from cone snail venom), cod-liver oil | Large, still under-explored source |
| **Minerals** | Kaolin, talc, bentonite, calcium carbonate, ferrous sulfate, sulfur; bhasmas of Ayurveda | Inorganic substances, mainly excipients or antacids |
| **Plant tissue culture** | Shikonin (from *Lithospermum* cell culture, produced commercially), paclitaxel by plant cell fermentation | Plant cells grown in sterile nutrient medium; supply independent of season and land |

## 1.5 Historical milestones in drug discovery

These eight drugs show how a natural product moves from traditional use to a pure medicine.

| Drug | Natural source | Key events | Importance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Morphine** | Latex of the unripe capsule of the opium poppy, *Papaver somniferum* (Papaveraceae) | Isolated by the German pharmacist **F. W. Sertürner** in the early 1800s; named after Morpheus, god of dreams | First alkaloid ever isolated; proved that a plant's action comes from a pure chemical; still a standard analgesic |
| **Quinine** | Bark of *Cinchona* species (Rubiaceae) | Bark used in South America for fevers; isolated by **Pelletier and Caventou** in 1820 | First effective treatment of malaria; led to synthetic antimalarials such as chloroquine |
| **Aspirin** | Willow bark (*Salix*) and meadowsweet (*Spiraea / Filipendula ulmaria*) | Salicin isolated from willow bark; salicylic acid made from it but irritated the stomach; **Felix Hoffmann** at Bayer made acetylsalicylic acid (1897) | First semisynthetic drug from a natural lead; name: "a" (acetyl) + "spir" (*Spiraea*) |
| **Warfarin** | Spoiled sweet clover (*Melilotus*) hay | Cattle bled to death after eating mouldy sweet clover; **K. P. Link** isolated the anticoagulant **dicoumarol**; warfarin was later made as a rat poison and then as a medicine | Oral anticoagulant; name from WARF (Wisconsin Alumni Research Foundation) + coumarin |
| **Penicillin** | Mould *Penicillium notatum* (now *P. chrysogenum*) | **Alexander Fleming** noticed in 1928 that the mould killed staphylococci; **Florey and Chain** purified it in the 1940s; Nobel Prize 1945 | First antibiotic; began the antibiotic era and modern fermentation industry |
| **Cephalosporin** | Fungus *Cephalosporium acremonium* (now *Acremonium chrysogenum*) | Found by **Giuseppe Brotzu** in sea water near a sewage outlet in Sardinia (1940s); cephalosporin C isolated later at Oxford | β-lactam antibiotics resistant to penicillinase; base for many generations of semisynthetic cephalosporins |
| **Taxol (paclitaxel)** | Bark of the Pacific yew, *Taxus brevifolia* (Taxaceae) | Found in a US National Cancer Institute plant screening programme; isolated by **Wall and Wani**; unique action of stabilising microtubules found later; now made semisynthetically from 10-deacetylbaccatin III in needles of *Taxus baccata* | Major anticancer drug (ovarian, breast cancer); classic case of conservation problem solved by semisynthesis |
| **Artemisinin** | Leaves of sweet wormwood, *Artemisia annua* (Asteraceae) — "qinghao" of Chinese medicine | **Tu Youyou** found it in the 1970s after reading an old Chinese text that advised steeping the herb in cold water; Nobel Prize 2015 | Sesquiterpene lactone with an endoperoxide bridge; artemisinin-based combinations are the standard treatment of falciparum malaria |

**Lessons from these milestones**: traditional knowledge points to the plant; isolation gives the pure compound; chemistry then improves it (aspirin, semisynthetic cephalosporins, paclitaxel); and supply problems lead to fermentation, semisynthesis or cultivation.

## 1.6 Herbal and traditional pharmacopoeias

A **pharmacopoeia** is an official book of standards that describes drugs (monographs) and the tests they must pass — identity, purity and strength.

| Pharmacopoeia | Published by | What it covers for herbal drugs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Indian Pharmacopoeia (IP)** | Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad (Ministry of Health and Family Welfare); first edition 1955, revised periodically | Legal standard under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act; includes a section of monographs on herbs and herbal products (identity by macroscopy, microscopy and TLC, ash values, extractive values, assay of marker compounds) |
| **British Herbal Pharmacopoeia (BHP)** | British Herbal Medicine Association | Monographs of herbs used by herbal practitioners: description, microscopy, identity tests, quantitative standards, action and indications |
| **United States Pharmacopeia – Herbal Medicines and Dietary Supplements** | United States Pharmacopeial Convention | Monographs for botanical dietary supplements and their extracts (for example ginkgo, garlic, turmeric); USP also publishes a separate Herbal Medicines Compendium for herbs used worldwide |
| **Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API)** | Pharmacopoeia Commission for Indian Medicine & Homoeopathy (PCIM&H), Ministry of AYUSH | Part I: single plant drugs; Part II: compound Ayurvedic formulations; gives Sanskrit name, identity, purity, TLC, and Ayurvedic properties (rasa, guna, virya, vipaka) |
| **Unani Pharmacopoeia of India (UPI)** | PCIM&H, Ministry of AYUSH | Single drugs and compound formulations of the Unani system, with Unani names and temperament (mizaj) |
| **American Herbal Pharmacopoeia (AHP)** | An independent non-government organisation in the USA | Detailed monographs with botany, analytical methods (HPTLC, HPLC), pharmacology and safety; not a legal standard but widely respected |

Similar official books exist for Siddha (Siddha Pharmacopoeia of India) and Homoeopathy (Homoeopathic Pharmacopoeia of India), also under PCIM&H.

## 1.7 Official and non-official drugs

- **Official drugs**: drugs that have a monograph in the official pharmacopoeia of a country (for India, the IP). They must meet those standards. Example: ispaghula husk, senna, clove in the IP.
- **Non-official (unofficial) drugs**: drugs not listed in the pharmacopoeia, though they may be well known and used. Example: many folk remedies, newer herbs.

## 1.8 Codified and non-codified drugs

- **Codified drugs**: drugs of traditional systems whose use is written down in authoritative classical texts — Ayurvedic, Unani, Siddha and Sowa-Rigpa texts. Their names, preparation and uses are standardised by tradition. Example: Triphala churna, Ashwagandharishta.
- **Non-codified drugs**: remedies passed on orally through folk, tribal and household practice, not written in classical texts. They are an important lead for ethnopharmacology and must be documented (for example in the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library, which protects Indian traditional knowledge from wrongful patents).

## 1.9 Classification of crude drugs

Crude drugs are arranged in a system so they can be studied and compared. Six systems are used.

### (a) Alphabetical classification

Drugs listed A to Z by their Latin or English name. Used in pharmacopoeias (IP, BP, USP) and dictionaries.

- Example: Acacia, Agar, Aloe, Belladonna, Benzoin, Cardamom, Clove …
- **Merits**: very easy to locate a drug; suits reference books.
- **Limitations**: no link between drugs; drugs from the same plant family, part or chemical group fall far apart.

### (b) Morphological classification

Drugs grouped by the plant or animal part used.

| Group | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| **Organised drugs** (have cell structure) | |
| Leaves | Senna, digitalis, vasaka, tulsi |
| Barks | Cinchona, cinnamon, arjuna |
| Roots and rhizomes | Rauwolfia, ginger, turmeric, ashwagandha |
| Flowers | Clove (buds), saffron (stigmas) |
| Fruits | Fennel, coriander, amla, chasteberry |
| Seeds | Nux vomica, ispaghula, fenugreek |
| Woods | Sandalwood, quassia |
| Whole herbs | Brahmi, kalmegh, chirata |
| **Unorganised drugs** (no cells) | Gums, resins, latex, dried juices (aloe), oils, waxes, extracts |

- **Merits**: helps learn identification (macroscopy and microscopy) because drugs of one group look alike; useful for practical study.
- **Limitations**: does not relate the drugs' chemistry or action; one plant may give several parts.

### (c) Taxonomical classification

Drugs arranged according to the natural plant classification: phylum → class → order → family → genus → species (systems of Bentham and Hooker, Engler and Prantl). Example: Solanaceae — belladonna, datura, hyoscyamus, ashwagandha; Apiaceae — fennel, coriander, cumin.

- **Merits**: shows natural relationships; plants of one family often have similar constituents (Solanaceae → tropane alkaloids).
- **Limitations**: not useful for therapeutic study; drugs of one family may have very different actions; classification changes when botanists revise families.

### (d) Chemical classification

Drugs grouped by their main active constituent.

| Chemical group | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Carbohydrates | Acacia, agar, ispaghula, starch |
| Proteins / enzymes | Papain, gelatin |
| Lipids | Castor oil, beeswax, wool fat |
| Alkaloids | Cinchona, belladonna, opium, vasaka |
| Glycosides | Senna, digitalis, aloe |
| Tannins | Catechu, myrobalan |
| Volatile oils | Clove, peppermint, eucalyptus |
| Resins | Benzoin, colophony, boswellia |

- **Merits**: links drugs of similar chemistry; suits phytochemical study and assay methods.
- **Limitations**: many drugs contain more than one important group (ginger has volatile oil and pungent resinous principles); constituents of some drugs are not fully known.

### (e) Pharmacological (therapeutic) classification

Drugs grouped by their action or use.

| Action | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Laxatives / purgatives | Senna, aloe, ispaghula, castor oil |
| Cardiotonics | Digitalis, arjuna |
| Expectorants | Vasaka, liquorice |
| Antimalarials | Cinchona, artemisia |
| Hepatoprotectives | Milk thistle, kutki |
| Anticancer | Catharanthus, taxus |
| Immunomodulators | Tulsi, giloy, ashwagandha |

- **Merits**: most useful for pharmacologists and prescribers; helps choose substitutes.
- **Limitations**: one drug may have several actions (garlic: antimicrobial and lipid-lowering); unrelated plants fall together.

### (f) Chemotaxonomic classification

Plants classified by both **botanical relationship and chemical constituents**, on the idea that related plants make related compounds. Example: tropane alkaloids in Solanaceae; isoquinoline alkaloids in Papaveraceae; iridoids in Plantaginaceae; caffeine-containing plants (tea, coffee, cola) from different families.

- **Merits**: most modern system; helps find new sources of a known compound and correct doubtful taxonomy.
- **Limitations**: needs full chemical data on many plants; a compound may appear in unrelated families; chemical content changes with environment.

## Remember

- Pharmacognosy = pharmakon (drug) + gnosis (knowledge); term usually credited to Seydler (1815).
- Sources: plants, animals, microbes, marine organisms, minerals and plant tissue culture.
- Morphine — first alkaloid (Sertürner); quinine — Pelletier and Caventou, 1820; aspirin — Hoffmann, 1897; dicoumarol from spoiled sweet clover → warfarin; penicillin — Fleming 1928; cephalosporin — Brotzu, Sardinia; taxol — *Taxus brevifolia*, microtubule stabiliser; artemisinin — Tu Youyou, *Artemisia annua*, Nobel 2015.
- IP — Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission; API and UPI — PCIM&H under Ministry of AYUSH.
- Official = in the pharmacopoeia; codified = written in classical texts of a traditional system.
- Six classifications: alphabetical, morphological (organised/unorganised), taxonomical, chemical, pharmacological, chemotaxonomic — learn one merit and one limitation for each.

# Unit 2: Cultivation, collection, processing and storage of drugs of natural origin

The quality of a herbal medicine is decided long before it reaches the factory. The seed, the soil, the time of harvest, the way the plant is dried and the store it waits in all change how much active constituent it holds. This unit covers how medicinal plants are grown and handled, the WHO rules for doing it well, how plant hormones and genetics can raise yield, and how threatened medicinal plants are conserved.

## 2.1 Why cultivate medicinal plants instead of collecting them wild?

| Wild collection | Cultivation |
| --- | --- |
| Plants vary in age, chemotype and constituent content | Uniform, known variety; steady quality |
| Risk of wrong species and adulteration | Correct identity from authenticated seed |
| Over-harvesting endangers species (kutki, chirata, sarpagandha) | Protects wild populations |
| Supply depends on season and forest access | Planned, regular supply |
| Contamination hard to control | Pesticides, heavy metals and microbes can be controlled |
| Cheap labour, no land cost | Needs land, inputs and expertise |

## 2.2 Methods of plant cultivation (propagation)

### (a) Sexual method — by seeds

New plants grow from seeds. Used for annuals and plants that set seed well: fennel, coriander, isabgol (*Plantago ovata*), datura, ashwagandha, tulsi, fenugreek.

- **Merits**: cheap, easy, many plants at once, seeds store and transport well, plants are long-lived and hardy.
- **Demerits**: offspring vary (cross-pollination), so constituent content varies; slower to mature; some seeds have poor germination or dormancy.
- Seed treatment to improve germination: soaking in water, scarification (scratching a hard coat, or treating with acid), stratification (cold treatment), gibberellic acid.

### (b) Asexual (vegetative) method

A part of the plant other than seed gives a new plant identical to the parent (a clone). Used to keep a high-yielding plant true to type.

| Method | How it works | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Natural** — rhizomes | Pieces of rhizome with buds are planted | Ginger, turmeric |
| Bulbs | Bulbs or cloves planted | Garlic, onion |
| Tubers / tuberous roots | Planted with an eye or bud | Potato (tubers), sweet potato and dahlia (tuberous roots) |
| Runners and suckers | Stems that root where they touch the soil | Mint (runners), banana (suckers) |
| **Artificial** — cuttings | A piece of stem, root or leaf is planted and forms roots | Stem: rose, mint; root: rauwolfia |
| Layering | A branch is made to root while still on the parent, then cut off; air layering (gootee) wraps a wounded branch in moist moss | Lemon, guava, jasmine |
| Grafting | The scion (upper shoot of a good variety) is joined to the rootstock of a hardy plant | Mango, citrus, cinchona (to combine vigour and alkaloid yield) |
| Budding | Only a bud of the good variety is inserted in the rootstock | Rose, citrus |
| **Micropropagation** (tissue culture) | Small pieces (explants) grown on sterile medium with hormones give thousands of identical plantlets | Rare and slow-growing medicinal plants, kutki, stevia |

- **Merits of vegetative propagation**: true-to-type, uniform chemistry; faster maturity; useful for plants with no or poor seed.
- **Demerits**: costlier, plants may be shorter-lived, diseases pass from parent to offspring.

## 2.3 Factors influencing cultivation

| Factor | Effect | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Altitude** | Some plants need hills, others plains | Tea and cinchona grow well on hills; kutki and chirata are high-altitude Himalayan plants |
| **Temperature** | Controls growth and secondary metabolism; frost kills tropical plants | Volatile oil content of mint varies with temperature |
| **Rainfall and irrigation** | Water stress can raise or lower constituents; waterlogging rots roots | Isabgol needs dry weather at maturity |
| **Day length and light** | Flowering and many metabolites depend on light | Shade lowers volatile oil in some herbs |
| **Soil** | Texture (sandy, clay, loam), pH, drainage and nutrients | Root drugs prefer loose, well-drained soil |
| **Fertilisers / manures** | N, P, K and organic manure raise biomass; nitrogen often raises alkaloid content | Nitrogen feeding raises tropane alkaloids in belladonna |
| **Pests and diseases** | Damage yield; pesticides leave residues | Organic or integrated pest management preferred |
| **Genetic make-up** | Chemical races (chemotypes) of one species differ | Oil composition of tulsi chemotypes |

## 2.4 Collection

The right **time** and **part** matter because constituent levels change with age and season.

| Part | Best time of collection |
| --- | --- |
| Leaves and herbs | When the plant is flowering or just before, when photosynthesis is most active (senna, vasaka, tulsi) |
| Flowers | Before or just at full opening (clove is collected as buds) |
| Fruits | When fully grown; ripe or unripe as required (amla when ripe) |
| Seeds | When fully ripe and dry |
| Barks | In spring, when the cambium is active and the bark peels off easily (cinchona, arjuna) |
| Roots and rhizomes | After the aerial parts die down (late autumn/winter), when food reserves are stored |
| Gums and resins | In the dry season, by making cuts in the bark (acacia gum, boswellia) |

- Collection should be by trained people who know the plant, with clean tools, avoiding damaged or diseased plants and foreign matter.
- Collect only a fraction of a wild population and leave enough to regenerate (sustainable harvesting).

## 2.5 Processing

After collection the material is prepared so it keeps well.

1. **Garbling (cleaning)**: removing soil, stones, other plant parts and foreign organic matter. Example: removing stalks from clove.
2. **Washing** (for roots) and **cutting/slicing** to speed drying.
3. **Special treatments**: peeling (ginger, liquorice), fermentation or "curing" to develop flavour (vanilla, tea), parboiling (turmeric is boiled before drying), sweating.
4. **Drying**: the most important step. It removes water so that enzymes and microbes cannot act.

| Drying method | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Sun drying | Seeds, barks, roots (cheap but uneven, contamination risk) |
| Shade drying | Leaves, flowers and drugs with volatile oil or colour (tulsi, mint) to protect volatile and light-sensitive constituents |
| Artificial (hot-air ovens, tray driers) | Controlled temperature and time; aromatic drugs are dried at low temperature |
| Freeze-drying / vacuum drying | Heat-sensitive material and enzymes |

Some drugs need enzyme action to develop their principle before drying (vanilla, where glucovanillin breaks down to vanillin during curing); others must be dried quickly to stop enzymes destroying the glycoside (digitalis).

5. **Grading and packing**: sorting by size, colour and quality; packing in suitable containers with labels.

## 2.6 Storage

Badly stored drugs lose activity, gain moisture and get mouldy or insect-infested.

**Factors that spoil stored drugs**: moisture, heat, light, air (oxygen), microbes, insects (beetles, moths) and rodents.

**Good storage practice**

- Store in clean, dry, cool, well-ventilated stores, away from direct light.
- Use well-closed or airtight containers; hygroscopic drugs (squill, digitalis) are kept with a desiccant.
- Drugs with volatile oil in airtight, well-filled containers.
- Light-sensitive drugs in amber or opaque containers.
- Protect from insects by cleanliness and, where permitted, by fumigation; protect from rodents.
- First-in, first-out stock rotation; label with name, batch and date of collection.
- Check moisture content and look for mould and insects at intervals.

## 2.7 Good Agricultural and Collection Practices (GACP)

The **WHO guidelines on Good Agricultural and Collection Practices (GACP) for medicinal plants** (2003) set rules so that herbal raw material is safe and of uniform quality. India's National Medicinal Plants Board has similar GAP and GFCP (good field collection practice) guidelines.

**Main points of GACP**

1. **Identification**: correct botanical identity of seeds and planting material; voucher specimens kept.
2. **Seeds and propagation material**: authentic, free from disease and contamination.
3. **Site selection**: soil and water free from heavy metals, pesticides and pollution; past use of the land known.
4. **Climate**: suited to the species.
5. **Soil, fertiliser and irrigation**: properly composted manure only (no human faeces); clean irrigation water.
6. **Crop maintenance and protection**: minimum pesticide use, only approved agents, records kept.
7. **Harvest**: at the right time for best quality; clean equipment; avoid wet weather.
8. **Wild collection**: permits, sustainable quantities, protection of endangered species.
9. **Primary processing**: prompt cleaning and drying, separate from contaminants.
10. **Packaging, storage and transport**: clean, labelled, protected.
11. **Personnel**: trained, healthy workers with hygiene and protective clothing.
12. **Documentation**: every step recorded so the batch can be traced (traceability), and quality assurance by audit.

## 2.8 Plant hormones and their applications

**Plant hormones (phytohormones)** are organic substances made in small amounts in one part of a plant that control growth or development elsewhere. Synthetic ones with the same effect are called plant growth regulators.

| Hormone | Examples | Main effects | Use in cultivation of medicinal plants |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Auxins** | Indole-3-acetic acid (IAA, natural), indole-3-butyric acid (IBA), naphthalene acetic acid (NAA), 2,4-D | Cell elongation, root formation, apical dominance | Rooting of stem cuttings; callus induction in tissue culture; 2,4-D as a weedicide at higher strength |
| **Gibberellins** | Gibberellic acid (GA3) | Stem elongation, breaking seed dormancy, flowering, fruit growth | Better germination and larger biomass; GA treatment is reported to change alkaloid and volatile-oil yield in some crops |
| **Cytokinins** | Kinetin, zeatin, benzylaminopurine (BAP) | Cell division, shoot formation, delay of ageing | Shoot multiplication in micropropagation (with auxin: high auxin → roots, high cytokinin → shoots) |
| **Abscisic acid (ABA)** | ABA | Dormancy, stomatal closure, stress response | Stress signalling that can switch on secondary metabolism |
| **Ethylene** | Ethylene gas; ethephon (releases ethylene) | Fruit ripening, leaf fall, flowering | Ethephon increases latex flow in rubber; ripening of fruits |

Related signal molecules such as **jasmonic acid / methyl jasmonate** and **salicylic acid** act as **elicitors**: they switch on defence pathways and are used in cell cultures to raise secondary metabolite yield.

## 2.9 Polyploidy, mutation and hybridisation

These genetic methods produce plants with more of the desired secondary metabolite.

### (a) Polyploidy

Having more than two sets of chromosomes (triploid 3n, tetraploid 4n …).

- Produced by treating seeds or growing tips with **colchicine** (from *Colchicum autumnale*), which stops spindle formation so the chromosome number doubles.
- Polyploids often have larger organs (leaves, flowers, seeds) and may have higher constituent content.
- **Examples**: tetraploid *Datura* strains with higher alkaloid content; in *Acorus calamus* (sweet flag) the diploid American form has almost no β-asarone, while triploid and tetraploid (Indian) forms are rich in it — so ploidy controls chemistry.

### (b) Mutation

A sudden heritable change in a gene or chromosome.

- Induced by **physical mutagens** (X-rays, gamma rays, UV light) or **chemical mutagens** (ethyl methanesulfonate, nitrosoguanidine, colchicine).
- Mutants are screened and high-yielding ones kept.
- **Examples**: repeated mutation and selection of *Penicillium chrysogenum* raised penicillin yield many-fold over Fleming's strain; poppy lines that accumulate thebaine instead of morphine; mutant mint strains resistant to wilt.

### (c) Hybridisation

Crossing two plants of different varieties or species to combine their useful characters in the offspring.

- **Examples**: peppermint (*Mentha × piperita*) is itself a hybrid of water mint and spearmint; hybrids of *Cinchona ledgeriana* (high alkaloid) and *C. succirubra* (vigorous) give good yield and hardiness; high-yielding hybrid varieties of many crops.
- **Hybrid vigour (heterosis)**: hybrids often grow faster and bigger than both parents.

## 2.10 Conservation of medicinal plants

Most Indian medicinal plants used by industry are still collected from the wild, and many are threatened. The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List grades threat (critically endangered, endangered, vulnerable); CITES controls international trade in listed species; the **National Medicinal Plants Board (NMPB)** under the Ministry of AYUSH supports cultivation and conservation; the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 regulates access and benefit-sharing.

| | In-situ conservation | Ex-situ conservation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Meaning | Protecting plants in their **natural habitat** | Protecting plants **outside** their natural habitat |
| Methods | National parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, sacred groves, Medicinal Plants Conservation Areas (MPCAs) | Botanical and herbal gardens, field gene banks, seed banks, tissue culture banks, cryopreservation (storage in liquid nitrogen at −196 °C), cultivation on farms |
| Merits | Whole ecosystem and natural evolution preserved; cheap per species | Rescue of very rare species; material available for research and planting back |
| Limits | Needs protection from people and grazing; habitat loss | Limited genetic variety; costly; plants lose adaptation to the wild |

## 2.11 Strategies for value addition

Value addition means turning raw herbs into products worth more, so that growers earn more and have a reason to cultivate rather than over-collect.

- Good primary processing (cleaning, drying, grading) to fetch a higher price.
- Making standardised extracts, oils, powders and formulations.
- Organic and GACP certification; geographical indication tags.
- Farmer producer organisations and contract farming with industry (buy-back).
- Using renewable parts (leaves, fruits) instead of roots where the action allows.
- Developing nutraceuticals, cosmetics and export products.

## 2.12 Eco-pharmacognosy

**Eco-pharmacognosy** is the study and practice of using natural resources for medicines in a sustainable, environmentally friendly way, so that the plants will still be available to future generations. Its main ideas:

1. Know which species are threatened and how much can safely be harvested.
2. Shift from wild collection to cultivation.
3. Use biotechnology (tissue culture, cell culture) to produce compounds without destroying plants.
4. Use renewable parts and avoid destructive harvesting of roots and barks.
5. Prevent waste and ensure fair sharing of benefits with the local communities who hold the knowledge.
6. Standardise products so less raw material is needed for the same effect.

### Example 1: Kutki

- **Biological source**: rhizomes and roots of *Picrorhiza kurroa*, family Plantaginaceae (formerly Scrophulariaceae).
- Grows in the alpine Himalaya at high altitude; slow-growing.
- Constituents: bitter iridoid glycosides — **picroside I, picroside II** and **kutkoside** (the mixture is called **kutkin**).
- Use: liver protection, bitter tonic.
- **Threat**: the whole underground part is dug up, so heavy trade has made it threatened in the wild.
- **Conservation**: cultivation in Himalayan states, micropropagation, nursery raising of planting stock, sustainable harvesting limits, and in-situ protection in high-altitude reserves.

### Example 2: Chirata

- **Biological source**: dried whole plant of *Swertia chirayita*, family Gentianaceae.
- Grows in the temperate Himalaya.
- Constituents: very bitter secoiridoid glycosides — **amarogentin**, **swertiamarin**, gentiopicrin — and xanthones such as **mangiferin**.
- Use: bitter tonic, fever, appetite, liver.
- **Threat**: the whole plant is uprooted before seeds set; widespread adulteration with other *Swertia* species also shows the shortage.
- **Conservation**: seed-based cultivation, tissue culture, harvesting only after seed fall, and community-based conservation.

## Remember

- Seeds → variable but cheap; vegetative propagation → true-to-type clones (cuttings, layering, grafting, budding, rhizomes, bulbs, micropropagation).
- Collection times: leaves at flowering; barks in spring; roots after aerial parts die; flowers before full bloom; gums in dry season.
- Drying stops enzyme and microbial action; shade-dry aromatic and coloured drugs.
- WHO GACP (2003): identity, site, cultivation, harvest, processing, personnel, documentation.
- Auxins → roots; gibberellins → elongation and germination; cytokinins → shoots/cell division; ABA → dormancy; ethylene → ripening; jasmonate → elicitor.
- Colchicine doubles chromosomes (polyploidy); *Acorus calamus* ploidy changes β-asarone; mutation raised penicillin yield; peppermint is a natural hybrid.
- In-situ = natural habitat (sacred groves, MPCAs); ex-situ = gardens, seed banks, cryopreservation.
- Kutki (*Picrorhiza kurroa*, picrosides) and chirata (*Swertia chirayita*, amarogentin, swertiamarin) are threatened Himalayan bitters — protected by cultivation and sustainable harvest (eco-pharmacognosy).
